title: Democracy vs Authoritarianism
hook: The deepest dividing line between regimes isn't left versus right — it's whether power can be lost. Can the people remove their rulers, or not?
key_points: Democracies feature competitive elections, real limits on power, and protected rights.
Authoritarian regimes concentrate power and block genuine challenges to those who hold it.
Key test: can rulers be peacefully removed, and is there meaningful opposition and free press?
Many states are hybrids — holding elections that look democratic but are not genuinely free or fair.
content_html: Regimes are often sorted along a left-right economic axis, but a more fundamental distinction concerns the location and limits of power itself. The question that separates democracy from authoritarianism is deceptively simple: can those who govern be removed by those they govern? In a democracy the answer is yes — through competitive elections in which the outcome is genuinely uncertain, with real limits on what winners can do and protected rights for everyone, including the losers. In an authoritarian regime the answer is effectively no: power is concentrated, and genuine challenges to the rulers are blocked, whether by banning opposition, controlling the courts, or muzzling the press.
extra_html: Encyclopaedia Britannica describes authoritarianism as a system in which power is concentrated in a leader or small group not constitutionally accountable to the people. The practical markers of the divide are concrete: is there meaningful opposition that can win, an independent judiciary, and a free press able to criticize the government? A crucial complication is that the line is now often blurred. Many modern states are hybrids — sometimes called "competitive authoritarian" or "illiberal" regimes — that hold elections looking democratic on the surface while quietly rigging the conditions: capturing the media, harassing opponents, or packing the courts. Recognizing these hybrids matters, because they borrow democracy's legitimacy without accepting its central rule that power must be genuinely losable.

related.title: What Democracy Means
related.hook: Rule by the people: a system where political power ultimately traces back to citizens, usually through regular, free elections.

related.title: Monarchies, Republics & Regime Types
related.hook: Is the head of state a queen or a president? That old question — monarchy or republic — turns out to matter less than whether real power is elected and accountable.

related.title: The Free Press & Democracy
related.hook: A free press is sometimes called the "fourth estate" — an unofficial branch of power whose job is to watch the other three on the public's behalf.

related.title: Democratic Backsliding
related.hook: Democracies rarely die in a single coup anymore. More often they erode — legally, gradually, step by step — until little is left but the shell of elections.

related.title: Electoral vs Liberal Democracy
related.hook: Holding elections isn't the whole of democracy. Without rights, courts, and limits on the winner, voting alone can deliver an elected strongman.

flashcards.prompt: What is the clearest test separating democracy from authoritarianism?
flashcards.back_html: Whether rulers can be peacefully removed — democracies allow genuine competition and turnover; authoritarian regimes block real challenges to power.

flashcards.prompt: Which feature is characteristic of an authoritarian regime?

choices.text: Concentrated power with no genuine way to challenge those who hold it
Competitive elections with a free press and protected opposition
Independent courts that routinely overrule the leader

flashcards.explanation_html: Authoritarian rule concentrates power and suppresses real opposition, so those in charge cannot be effectively removed.

flashcards.prompt: Why can holding elections alone fail to make a regime democratic?

choices.text: Hybrid regimes can stage elections that aren't genuinely free or fair
Democracies are forbidden from holding elections
Elections always guarantee an opposition victory

flashcards.explanation_html: Many states hold elections for legitimacy while controlling the media, courts, or vote — the form of democracy without the substance.
